subtopic_detail: Interpreting discordant cytomegalovirus avidity and immunoglobulin results in the first trimester
stem:
You are the registrar in an antenatal clinic. A 26-year-old childcare worker at 13 weeks in her first pregnancy had serology sent by her general practitioner after 10 days of fatigue and mildly tender neck glands that have now resolved.

She has a well 2-year-old nephew in her care 3 days a week. She has had no rash, no sore throat and no jaundice. She takes pregnancy multivitamins only.

Cytomegalovirus immunoglobulin M is positive, immunoglobulin G is positive, and immunoglobulin G avidity is reported as high. Epstein-Barr virus serology shows past infection. Liver function tests, full blood count and film are within normal limits. Toxoplasma immunoglobulin M is negative. An ultrasound at 13 weeks shows a single foetus with crown rump length consistent with dates, normal nuchal translucency, and no intracranial or abdominal abnormality identified.

data_table.Investigations: Cytomegalovirus immunoglobulin M positive, immunoglobulin G positive, immunoglobulin G avidity high. Epstein-Barr virus serology shows past infection. Toxoplasma immunoglobulin M negative. Liver function tests, full blood count and film within normal limits. Ultrasound at 13 weeks: crown rump length consistent with dates, normal nuchal translucency, no intracranial or abdominal abnormality

lead_in: What is the most appropriate interpretation and next step?

options.text: Infection occurred before conception; give hygiene advice and continue routine antenatal care with a morphology scan
options.rationale: High immunoglobulin G avidity in the first trimester indicates that infection occurred more than about 3 months earlier, which places it before conception and means the foetus is not at risk from that episode. Persistent immunoglobulin M is common for months after infection and is the reason avidity testing exists, so the discordance resolves in favour of past infection. (Source: RANZCOG: Cytomegalovirus in pregnancy)

options.text: Primary infection has occurred in pregnancy; arrange amniocentesis for viral polymerase chain reaction after 21 weeks
options.rationale: Amniocentesis is the correct investigation for confirmed primary infection during pregnancy, but the high avidity result here excludes recent infection. It would be indicated if avidity were low or if seroconversion from a negative immunoglobulin G had been documented. (Source: RANZCOG: Cytomegalovirus in pregnancy)

options.text: Primary infection has occurred in pregnancy; commence oral valaciclovir and arrange serial foetal neurosonography
options.rationale: High dose valaciclovir is an emerging option to reduce vertical transmission after confirmed periconceptional or first trimester primary infection, which has not occurred here. Treatment would be considered only once recent primary infection were established by low avidity or documented seroconversion. (Source: RANZCOG: Cytomegalovirus in pregnancy)

options.text: The results are uninterpretable; repeat the full serology panel in 3 weeks before giving any advice or counselling
options.rationale: Paired testing is valuable when avidity is intermediate or unavailable, but a clearly high avidity result in the first trimester is already conclusive and repeating it delays reassurance. Repeat testing would be appropriate for an intermediate avidity index or an equivocal immunoglobulin G. (Source: RANZCOG: Cytomegalovirus in pregnancy)

options.text: Reactivation has occurred in pregnancy; arrange monthly foetal growth ultrasound and neonatal hearing assessment only
options.rationale: Non-primary infection carries a much lower transmission risk than primary infection and does not warrant monthly growth surveillance in a structurally normal foetus. The described serology fits resolved past primary infection rather than active reactivation, which would not typically produce a symptomatic illness. (Source: RANZCOG: Cytomegalovirus in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Cytomegalovirus is the most common congenital infection and the leading infectious cause of childhood sensorineural hearing loss, so serology results generate considerable anxiety and are frequently misinterpreted. The central problem is that immunoglobulin M is neither sensitive nor specific for recent infection: it can persist for six to nine months after primary infection, can reappear during reactivation, and can be falsely positive through cross-reactivity with other herpesviruses. Avidity testing solves this by measuring how tightly immunoglobulin G binds antigen, which increases as the antibody response matures, so high avidity in early pregnancy places the infection before conception. Vertical transmission risk after primary infection is roughly 30 to 40 per cent and is highest with first trimester infection, whereas non-primary infection carries a risk closer to 1 to 2 per cent. Australia does not screen routinely, so hygiene counselling for women in contact with young children remains the main preventive strategy.
key_points: Immunoglobulin M persists for months and cross-reacts, so it cannot date an infection alone
High immunoglobulin G avidity indicates infection more than about 3 months earlier
Primary infection carries roughly 30 to 40 per cent vertical transmission; non-primary infection is far lower
Amniocentesis for viral polymerase chain reaction is deferred until after 21 weeks and at least 6 weeks from infection
Routine antenatal screening is not performed in Australia; hygiene advice is the preventive measure
explanation.pearls: Amniotic fluid polymerase chain reaction is falsely negative if taken before 21 weeks, because foetal diuresis must be established for virus to appear in the amniotic fluid at detectable levels.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Congenital cytomegalovirus infection

subtopic_detail: Primary amenorrhoea with absent uterus on imaging and normal female androgen levels
stem:
You are the registrar in an adolescent gynaecology clinic. A 16-year-old girl attends because she has never menstruated while all her friends began years ago. She has no cyclical pain and no abdominal swelling.

She is a competitive swimmer training 6 hours a week and eats well, with a stable weight. She has no headaches and no visual symptoms, and her sense of smell is normal.

On examination breast development is Tanner stage 5, axillary and pubic hair are Tanner stage 5, and height is on the 70th centile. The external genitalia are normal in appearance with a short blind-ending vaginal dimple. Pelvic ultrasound reports no uterus identified, with two normal ovaries containing antral follicles. Follicle stimulating hormone is 5.2 IU/L, luteinising hormone is 4.8 IU/L, oestradiol is in the mid-follicular range, and total testosterone is 1.2 nmol/L (0.5-1.7 female reference range). Renal tract ultrasound shows a solitary right kidney.

data_table.Examination: Breast Tanner stage 5, axillary and pubic hair Tanner stage 5, height 70th centile, normal external genitalia with a short blind-ending vaginal dimple
data_table.Investigations: Pelvic ultrasound: no uterus identified, two normal ovaries with antral follicles. Follicle stimulating hormone 5.2 IU/L, luteinising hormone 4.8 IU/L, oestradiol mid-follicular range, total testosterone 1.2 nmol/L (0.5-1.7 female range). Renal tract ultrasound: solitary right kidney

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Complete androgen insensitivity with intra-abdominal testes and absent Mullerian derivatives
options.rationale: Androgen insensitivity produces testosterone in the male range and absent or very sparse pubic and axillary hair because hair growth depends on androgen receptor function, whereas this girl has full Tanner stage 5 sexual hair and female range testosterone. The near-pair distinction is that both conditions give an absent uterus and a blind vagina, but only androgen insensitivity gives male range androgens. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea in adolescents)

options.text: Congenital absence of the Mullerian duct derivatives with normally functioning ovaries
options.rationale: Female range testosterone with normal ovaries containing antral follicles and normal gonadotrophins establishes a 46,XX individual whose ovaries are working, so the absent uterus reflects failure of Mullerian duct development rather than androgen effect. The associated solitary kidney supports this, because the Mullerian and mesonephric systems develop in close association and renal anomalies accompany roughly a third of cases. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea in adolescents)

options.text: Functional hypothalamic suppression from athletic training with reduced gonadotrophin secretion
options.rationale: Hypothalamic suppression gives low or low-normal gonadotrophins with low oestradiol and, critically, leaves the uterus present on imaging. It would explain secondary amenorrhoea in an athlete with a normal pelvic ultrasound and relative energy deficiency. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea in adolescents)

options.text: Gonadal dysgenesis with streak gonads and elevated gonadotrophin secretion from absent feedback
options.rationale: Streak gonads produce little oestradiol, so gonadotrophins rise markedly and spontaneous breast development does not occur without replacement. Here the ovaries contain antral follicles and gonadotrophins are normal, which excludes primary gonadal failure. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea in adolescents)

options.text: Transverse vaginal septum obstructing outflow above a normally developed uterine cavity
options.rationale: An obstructing septum leaves the uterus present and causes cyclical pain with accumulating blood, neither of which is present here. It would be the diagnosis in a girl with cyclical pain, a pelvic mass and a uterus visible on imaging. (Source: RANZCOG: Amenorrhoea in adolescents)

explanation.summary: Mullerian agenesis is the second most common cause of primary amenorrhoea after gonadal dysgenesis, and it is diagnosed by the combination of normal secondary sexual characteristics, an absent uterus and female range androgens. The ovaries are derived from a different embryological origin and function normally, which means the girl ovulates, experiences no hormonal deficiency and needs no hormone replacement, points that are genuinely reassuring and often not explained clearly at diagnosis. Because the Mullerian ducts develop adjacent to the mesonephric system, renal anomalies such as a solitary or pelvic kidney occur in around a third of cases and skeletal anomalies in a smaller proportion, so imaging of the renal tract is part of the assessment. Management centres on creating vaginal length, usually with graduated dilator therapy as first-line and surgery reserved for failure, alongside psychological support. Fertility is possible through retrieval of the woman's own oocytes with gestational surrogacy, which is legally permitted on an altruistic basis in Australia.
key_points: Normal breast and sexual hair development with an absent uterus and female androgens defines Mullerian agenesis
Female range testosterone and normal sexual hair distinguish it from complete androgen insensitivity
Ovaries are of separate embryological origin, so ovulation and hormone production are normal
Renal anomalies accompany roughly a third of cases, warranting renal tract imaging
Graduated vaginal dilators are first-line management, with surgery reserved for dilator failure
explanation.pearls: Pubic and axillary hair is the bedside discriminator: it is fully developed in Mullerian agenesis and sparse or absent in complete androgen insensitivity, because sexual hair growth requires functioning androgen receptors.

subtopic_detail: Timing of antenatal deinfibulation planning for a woman with type 3 genital cutting
stem:
You are the registrar in a hospital antenatal clinic. A 23-year-old woman who arrived in Australia 2 years ago attends at 20 weeks in her first pregnancy, accompanied by a professional interpreter she has agreed to.

She reports that passing urine takes several minutes and that periods before this pregnancy were prolonged and painful. She has no dysuria and no fever. She has not had intercourse difficulties raised as a concern by her or her partner.

On examination, with her consent, the vulva shows a horizontal band of scar tissue covering the introitus with a posterior opening admitting one fingertip. The urethral meatus is not visible. There is no tenderness, no discharge and no infection. The uterus is consistent with dates and foetal heart tones are normal. She says she does not know what was done to her as a child and asks what this will mean for the birth.

data_table.Examination: Horizontal band of scar tissue covering the introitus with a posterior opening admitting one fingertip, urethral meatus not visible, no tenderness, discharge or infection, uterus consistent with dates, foetal heart tones normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan?

options.text: Defer any procedure and plan deinfibulation during the second stage of labour with continuity of care arranged
options.rationale: Deinfibulation in the second stage is an acceptable fallback when a woman presents late or declines earlier intervention, but it is performed under time pressure with less opportunity for genuine consent. It would be the plan for a woman first seen in advanced labour. (Source: RANZCOG: Female genital mutilation)

options.text: Recommend planned caesarean section at 39 weeks to avoid vaginal birth, with continuity of care arranged
options.rationale: Previous genital cutting is not in itself an indication for caesarean birth, and recommending one avoids rather than addresses the obstruction while committing her to abdominal surgery in every future pregnancy. Caesarean birth would be indicated for a standard obstetric reason arising independently. (Source: RANZCOG: Female genital mutilation)

options.text: Discuss and offer planned antenatal deinfibulation in the second trimester with continuity of care arranged
options.rationale: Elective deinfibulation before labour allows the procedure to be done with adequate analgesia, informed discussion and an interpreter, and it permits vaginal examination, catheterisation and foetal scalp access during labour. The second trimester is the preferred window because the pregnancy is established and there is time to heal well before birth. (Source: RANZCOG: Female genital mutilation)

options.text: Arrange reinfibulation to be performed after the birth if she requests it, with continuity of care arranged
options.rationale: Reinfibulation is unlawful in all Australian jurisdictions and must not be performed or promised regardless of a woman's request, though the request itself deserves a respectful explanation. Repair after birth restores the anatomy to its deinfibulated state only. (Source: RANZCOG: Female genital mutilation)

options.text: Refer to the child protection team and defer any discussion of the birth plan until that assessment concludes
options.rationale: Mandatory reporting obligations concern girls at risk of cutting rather than adult women who were cut as children overseas, so notification here is not triggered by her own history. A report would be required if there were concern that a child in the family was at risk of undergoing the procedure. (Source: RANZCOG: Female genital mutilation)

explanation.summary: Type 3 cutting, in which the introitus is narrowed by an occlusive seal, creates specific obstetric problems: vaginal examination, catheterisation and foetal scalp electrode placement may be impossible, and labouring against a rigid scar risks anterior tears involving the urethra and severe perineal trauma. Deinfibulation divides the scar tissue anteriorly to expose the urethral meatus and restore access, and it is best done electively in the second trimester when it can be planned with the woman rather than improvised. Doing it antenatally also allows the conversation to happen properly, with a professional interpreter rather than a family member, since women frequently do not know what was done to them and have never been offered an explanation. Chronic sequelae including obstructed urinary flow, dysmenorrhoea, recurrent infection and dyspareunia are common and often never raised, so the antenatal visit is a genuine opportunity. Reinfibulation is a criminal offence throughout Australia, and declining it requires a clear and non-judgemental explanation.
key_points: Type 3 cutting obstructs examination, catheterisation and foetal monitoring during labour
Elective second trimester deinfibulation is preferred to intrapartum division
Previous genital cutting alone is not an indication for caesarean birth
Reinfibulation is unlawful in all Australian jurisdictions
Use a professional interpreter rather than a family member for these discussions
explanation.pearls: Mandatory reporting in this context is triggered by risk to a girl in the family, not by an adult woman's own history, so ask specifically about daughters and planned overseas travel rather than notifying on the basis of the woman's examination.

sources.label: Department of Health: Female genital mutilation in Australia

subtopic_detail: Classifying and siting repair of a perineal injury where external sphincter fibres are partly torn
stem:
You are the registrar called to the birth suite to assess a perineal injury after a 26-year-old woman's first birth. The baby weighed 4020 g and was born by vacuum extraction with a mediolateral episiotomy for a prolonged second stage.

The midwife has applied pressure and bleeding is controlled. The woman has a working epidural and is comfortable.

With her consent you examine in lithotomy in the birth suite with good lighting. The episiotomy extends through the perineal body. Digital rectal examination shows intact rectal mucosa and intact anal epithelium. On pill-rolling the external anal sphincter between index finger and thumb, you find the torn fibres involve less than half the thickness of the external sphincter across its width, and the internal anal sphincter appears intact as a separate pale layer. She has had no previous perineal injury and no anal incontinence.

data_table.Examination: Mediolateral episiotomy extending through the perineal body; rectal mucosa and anal epithelium intact; external anal sphincter torn through less than half its thickness; internal anal sphincter intact; bleeding controlled; epidural working

lead_in: How should this injury be classified and repaired?

options.text: Second degree tear involving the perineal body, repaired in the birth suite by an appropriately trained clinician
options.rationale: A second degree tear by definition spares the anal sphincter complex entirely, and here external sphincter fibres are divided. This classification would apply if pill-rolling had confirmed an intact external sphincter beneath a torn perineal body. (Source: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury

options.text: Third degree tear subclassified as 3b, repaired in an operating theatre by an appropriately trained clinician
options.rationale: The subclassification 3b denotes external sphincter disruption of more than half its thickness, whereas less than half is torn here. The near-pair distinction between 3a and 3b turns purely on the proportion of external sphincter thickness involved. (Source: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury

options.text: Third degree tear subclassified as 3c, repaired in an operating theatre by an appropriately trained clinician
options.rationale: The subclassification 3c requires the internal anal sphincter to be torn as well, and it is described here as an intact pale layer. Recognising internal sphincter involvement matters because it predicts worse continence outcomes than external disruption alone. (Source: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury

options.text: Third degree tear subclassified as 3a, repaired in an operating theatre by an appropriately trained clinician
options.rationale: Any disruption of the external anal sphincter makes this a third degree tear, and involvement of less than half its thickness defines the 3a subclassification. Sphincter repair requires theatre conditions with adequate lighting, assistance, anaesthesia and instruments, because repair quality in the birth suite is consistently poorer and long-term continence depends on it. (Source: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury

options.text: Fourth degree tear involving the anorectal complex, repaired in an operating theatre by an appropriately trained clinician
options.rationale: A fourth degree tear requires breach of the anal epithelium or rectal mucosa, both of which are explicitly intact on rectal examination. That classification would apply if the examining finger were visible through the wound or mucosa were divided. (Source: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury

explanation.summary: Obstetric anal sphincter injury is substantially underdiagnosed, and the single biggest determinant of whether it is found is whether a systematic rectal examination and pill-rolling of the sphincter are performed after every vaginal birth, not only when a tear looks deep. The classification is not academic: it drives where the repair happens, who performs it, what antibiotics and laxatives are prescribed, and what the woman is told about future births. Grades 3a and 3b differ only in the proportion of external sphincter thickness torn, while 3c adds internal sphincter disruption, which carries the worst prognosis for continence because the internal sphincter maintains resting tone. Repair in theatre with regional or general anaesthesia allows adequate relaxation and exposure, and either end-to-end or overlap technique is acceptable for the external sphincter, while the internal sphincter is repaired end-to-end separately. Postoperative care includes a single dose of broad spectrum antibiotics, laxatives to avoid straining, physiotherapy, and structured follow-up with symptom review before a subsequent pregnancy.
key_points: Any external anal sphincter disruption makes the tear third degree, regardless of perineal appearance
3a is less than half the external sphincter thickness, 3b more than half, 3c adds internal sphincter involvement
Fourth degree requires breach of the anal epithelium or rectal mucosa
Repair belongs in theatre with anaesthesia, lighting, assistance and appropriate instruments
Digital rectal examination and pill-rolling after every vaginal birth is what makes the diagnosis
explanation.pearls: Internal anal sphincter disruption, the 3c grade, is the finding that most strongly predicts long-term faecal urgency and incontinence, so identify it as a separate pale layer and repair it end-to-end rather than incorporating it into the external sphincter repair.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Prevention, detection and management of obstetric anal sphincter injury

subtopic_detail: Switching antithyroid drug between trimesters when hepatic and teratogenic risks conflict
stem:
You are the registrar in a joint obstetric medicine clinic. A 27-year-old woman at 13 weeks in her second pregnancy has Graves disease diagnosed 3 years ago and has taken propylthiouracil since her positive pregnancy test, switched from carbimazole by her general practitioner at 5 weeks.

She reports feeling well with no tremor and no palpitations. Her first child, born before her diagnosis, is well. She has no personal or family history of liver disease and drinks no alcohol.

Thyroid function today shows free thyroxine at the upper end of the pregnancy reference range and thyroid stimulating hormone suppressed at 0.03 mIU/L. Thyroid stimulating hormone receptor antibody is 8.2 IU/L (<1.8). Liver function tests taken today show alanine aminotransferase 186 U/L (<40), aspartate aminotransferase 152 U/L (<40), bilirubin 14 micromol/L (<20) and alkaline phosphatase within the pregnancy range. A repeat sample 4 days later confirms alanine aminotransferase 204 U/L. Viral hepatitis serology is negative and a liver ultrasound is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84/min, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Investigations: Free thyroxine at upper end of pregnancy reference range, thyroid stimulating hormone 0.03 mIU/L, thyroid stimulating hormone receptor antibody 8.2 IU/L (<1.8). Alanine aminotransferase 186 U/L then 204 U/L (<40), aspartate aminotransferase 152 U/L (<40), bilirubin 14 micromol/L (<20), alkaline phosphatase within pregnancy range. Viral hepatitis serology negative, liver ultrasound normal
data_table.Medications: Propylthiouracil since 5 weeks, switched from carbimazole

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue propylthiouracil at the current dose and monitor liver function and thyroid function closely
options.rationale: Propylthiouracil hepatotoxicity is idiosyncratic and can progress rapidly to hepatic failure requiring transplantation, so persisting with rising transaminases is not safe monitoring. Continuing would be defensible only in the first trimester if no alternative existed and liver enzymes were normal. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Stop all antithyroid medication now and monitor liver function and thyroid function closely
options.rationale: Uncontrolled thyrotoxicosis in pregnancy causes miscarriage, preterm birth, growth restriction and thyroid storm, and her antibody titre is high, so stopping treatment exchanges one risk for a larger one. Withdrawal would be reasonable in late pregnancy for a woman whose disease has remitted with a low antibody titre on a minimal dose. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Arrange radioactive iodine ablation after the first trimester and monitor thyroid function closely
options.rationale: Radioactive iodine is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy because it crosses the placenta and ablates the foetal thyroid from about 10 to 12 weeks when it begins concentrating iodine. It is an option for definitive treatment once pregnancy and breastfeeding are complete, with conception deferred for 6 months. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Add oral prednisolone to the current propylthiouracil and monitor liver function and thyroid function closely
options.rationale: Corticosteroid does not treat idiosyncratic drug induced liver injury and adding it leaves the offending agent in place while introducing glycaemic and infective risks. Prednisolone has a place in thyroid storm and in Graves orbitopathy, neither of which is present. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Switch back to carbimazole now and monitor liver function and thyroid function closely
options.rationale: Propylthiouracil is preferred in the first trimester to avoid carbimazole embryopathy, but that window has passed at 13 weeks and the guidance is to switch back to carbimazole for the remainder of pregnancy. Rising transaminases with other causes excluded make continuing propylthiouracil unsafe, since its hepatotoxicity can progress to fulminant failure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Managing Graves disease in pregnancy means trading two drug toxicities against each other across gestation. Carbimazole and its active metabolite methimazole are associated with an embryopathy including aplasia cutis, choanal and oesophageal atresia and abdominal wall defects, concentrated in the 6 to 10 week organogenesis window, which is why propylthiouracil is preferred in the first trimester. Propylthiouracil, however, carries a small but genuine risk of severe idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity that can progress to fulminant failure, and this risk does not diminish with time on the drug. The resulting strategy is to use propylthiouracil through the first trimester and then switch back, which many clinicians forget to do. Treatment aims to keep free thyroxine at or just above the upper limit of the pregnancy reference range on the lowest possible dose, deliberately accepting mild maternal hyperthyroidism, because both drugs cross the placenta and over-treatment causes foetal goitre and hypothyroidism.
key_points: Propylthiouracil in the first trimester avoids carbimazole embryopathy during organogenesis
Switch back to carbimazole after the first trimester because of propylthiouracil hepatotoxicity
Target free thyroxine at or just above the upper limit of the pregnancy range on the lowest effective dose
Radioactive iodine is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy and ablates the foetal thyroid
A receptor antibody titre more than three times the upper limit predicts foetal and neonatal thyrotoxicosis
explanation.pearls: Measure thyroid stimulating hormone receptor antibody at 18 to 22 weeks even in a woman rendered euthyroid or previously treated by surgery or ablation, because the antibody crosses the placenta and causes neonatal thyrotoxicosis independently of maternal thyroid status.
